This PR #43918 replaces public import with import in those cases where no additional downstream imports are then needed (and the changes doesn't otherwise cause an error).

This is a small step towards a full shake of public imports, essentially doing the "costless" piece. This is nevertheless a semantic change, as there is no guarantee that downstream users of Mathlib will not need to adjust their imports.

Nevertheless, I think this is worth doing!

I've checked that !bench is happy: there are a few changes I reverted because they did cause a slowdown, which I'll follow up on in separate PRs.

This PR will rot more or less instantly, so a quick decision on this would be very useful.
See also previous discussion from July in #mathlib4 > Privatization of imports

I think this PR is worth doing: we want to move in this direction eventually (that seems fairly clear to me, and is also shared among maintainers, I believe). How to get there is less clear, but this PR is a fairly uncontroversial step in this direction. I'll raise this in the reviewers stream, and if there are no objections will take a look at the diff (probably tomorrow/on Wednesday).
(update: the PR now removes public imports that can be removed with no additional imports in later files as well as demoting un-removable ones from public import to import.)
Isn't this update now going against the "don't needlessly prune transitive dependencies" rule we're had in the past?

I'm not convinced that has ever been a "rule", but yes, indeed, it goes against that expressed preference. :-)

I am happy to revert the public import deletions back to conversions to import, but it's not my preference, nor perhaps @Aaron Liu's and @Michael Rothgang's, from my reading of the review comments.

My understanding of the "don't needlessly prune transitive dependencies" rule was to avoid needless churn. In this case, I don't think this strongly applies - so I'd be inclined to approve it regardless.
My understanding is that is was meant to prevent future breakage in case the upstream imports are modified or removed
Any decisions on this? I would like to get this in, and am wasting time resolving merge conflicts.
Given the upvotes and lack of complaints I'm merging this @Kim Morrison

My Redhill project needed updating after this PR. Before, in KonyaginPrelude, I had

public import Mathlib.Analysis.SpecialFunctions.Pow.Real
public import Mathlib.RingTheory.Radical.NatInt
public import Redhill.Common.Conjectures

After I updated Redhill to include this landed PR, there was the error

Unknown constant `Int.prime_ofNat_iff`
Error code: lean.unknownIdentifier

and I had to absurdly include both an import and its transitive import:

import Mathlib.Analysis.SpecialFunctions.Pow.Real
import Mathlib.Data.Nat.Prime.Int -- this file
import Mathlib.RingTheory.Radical.NatInt -- is imported by this file
public import Redhill.Common.Conjectures

The problem is that even with public import Mathlib.RingTheory.Radical.NatInt I cannot use Int.prime_ofNat_iff, even though that lemma lives in Mathlib.Data.Nat.Prime.Int which is imported by Mathlib.RingTheory.Radical.NatInt
@Jeremy Tan, isn't this the whole point of not making imports public? I think this is a feature, not a bug. :-)
Why did I get the behaviour I observed? Not being able to implicitly use things in a transitive import feels so much like a bug

Isn't it just because there's no public import chain from Mathlib.RingTheory.Radical.NatInt back to Mathlib.Data.Nat.Prime.Int? A chain of imports that are not all public means that merely importing NatInt won't pull in things from Prime.Int.
I don't see why we should make this import private, if you're importing a file about prime factors and radicals in ℕ and ℤ you're likely going to need lemmas about primes in ℕ and ℤ.

The point of public/private import split is to allow downstream to also do public import Stuff.Def; import Stuff.Lemma, thus eventually reducing build time for everyone, right? As the most used upstream, Mathlib has to do it first to enable it, even though it makes it more verbose in downstream
As an extreme example, the challenge file doesn't need lemmas about primes when importing def of prime factors

How far are we going to go with this? As an extreme example, I don't want to eventually end up with something like

module

public import Mathlib.FieldTheory.Galois.Basic
public import Mathlib.LinearAlgebra.Basis.Defs
public import Mathlib.LinearAlgebra.LinearIndependent.Defs

import Mathlib.Algebra.BigOperators.Pi
import Mathlib.Algebra.Group.Basic
import Mathlib.Algebra.Group.Semigroup
import Mathlib.Algebra.GroupWithZero.NeZero
import Mathlib.Algebra.Module.PID
import Mathlib.Algebra.Module.Submodule.RestrictScalars
import Mathlib.Algebra.MvPolynomial.Funext
import Mathlib.Algebra.Polynomial.Degree.Operations
import Mathlib.Data.Fin.SuccPred
import Mathlib.Data.Fintype.EquivFin
import Mathlib.Data.Set.Prod
import Mathlib.FieldTheory.Finite.Basic
import Mathlib.LinearAlgebra.AnnihilatingPolynomial
import Mathlib.LinearAlgebra.Basis.VectorSpace
import Mathlib.LinearAlgebra.Dimension.Finite
import Mathlib.LinearAlgebra.Dual.Lemmas
import Mathlib.LinearAlgebra.FiniteDimensional.Lemmas
import Mathlib.LinearAlgebra.LinearIndependent.Basic
import Mathlib.LinearAlgebra.LinearIndependent.Lemmas
import Mathlib.LinearAlgebra.Matrix.Determinant.Basic
import Mathlib.LinearAlgebra.Matrix.Nondegenerate
import Mathlib.LinearAlgebra.Quotient.Basic
import Mathlib.RingTheory.AdjoinRoot
import Mathlib.RingTheory.Algebraic.Integral
import Mathlib.RingTheory.Finiteness.Cardinality
import Mathlib.RingTheory.SimpleRing.Basic
import Mathlib.Tactic.ByContra
import Mathlib.Tactic.Convert
import Mathlib.Tactic.SimpRw
import Mathlib.Tactic.TermCongr
import Mathlib.Tactic.Use
I tried removing various publics from imports in Redhill. It did not go well
Aaron Liu I would actually consider something like that a win.

Jireh Loreaux said:

Aaron Liu I would actually consider something like that a win.

How so?
We're reducing the number of things in public scope, and isolating them to a small number of files.

In practice those private imports would be spread over a large number of files, right? There's not suddenly going to be a point where you have to do a lot of private imports, if you do this transitively
Oh I see - in downstream projects you get this

Artie Khovanov said:

In practice those private imports would be spread over a large number of files, right? There's not suddenly going to be a point where you have to do a lot of private imports, if you do this transitively

These were all taken from a single file in mathlib, for which I looked at all the theorems it used and compiled the required imports into a list.

What do you mean by "if you do this transitively"?
If you do it for its imports, etc

oh, I was doing this under the assumption that it had already been done for the imports, if you don't do it for the imports then you won't need as many of the private imports (since they will be gotten transitively)

if you don't do it to the imports then this is enough

module

public import Mathlib.FieldTheory.Galois.Basic

import Mathlib.Algebra.Module.PID
import Mathlib.Algebra.MvPolynomial.Funext
import Mathlib.FieldTheory.Finite.Basic
import Mathlib.LinearAlgebra.AnnihilatingPolynonial
import Mathlib.LinearAlgebra.Dual.Lemmas
oh, huh, fair

Although I love the concept of this PR, I must complain that #min_imports hasn't yet been adapted to the module system: It still computes a minimal set of imports assuming all imports upstream are public (hence transitive), which guarantees that is useless for fixing the breakage from #43918. What I found myself having to do has been to add import Mathlib, squeeze the simp calls, etc... until I find out with my brain what it is that is now missing, and then replace import Mathlib with import Mathlib.FileContaining.WhatIsNowMissing.
It is very annoying guesswork and I wish we had fixed #min_imports before proceeding with #43918

I should also complain that we have had for a while now a convention on how to order public vs private imports (namely

public import A
public import C

import B
import D

) and that #43918 just introduced ~3000 violations to this convention.

I believe @Thomas Murrills has been working on revamping ImportGraph and friends :octopus:
Which includes #min_imports
(P.S., #norm_imports and an experimental version of #find_home have already landed, and #min_imports is next now that the module system infra is set up :grinning_face_with_smiling_eyes:)
Btw, I should note @Yaël Dillies that the formatting produced by #norm_imports follows this convention :) (I am hoping to make it a linter soon instead of a command...)
(Or at least I think it does! Let me know if you have opinions about meta spacing :grinning_face_with_smiling_eyes:)
Soon I will make an announcement post to make people aware of this tooling, but I am hoping to at least get #min_imports in first.

Yes, could we please not introduce arbitrary ordering requirements to get things done. @Yaël Dillies, if you want to work on #min_imports, that's great, please do so. Similarly, if you'd like a linter for ordering imports, that's great, obviously we will all follow it if it is linted, but otherwise this is off-topic for this PR.

I agree with the first part of your message, Kim --- but not the second one (as that convention is documented in our style guide). That said, the best fix there would be to auto-fix imports (to the extent this doesn't cause adverse performance impact etc.).
Ugh, lintable style guide requirements that aren't linted. Okay, I'll go do that.
I am already working on #min_imports?
Extending #norm_imports to be a linter is on my todo, but I won't block on it.
Is this style guide rule actually obeyed much in Mathlib? I suspect it is not. Given that there is now active work on upgrading this to a linter, could we please not consider it a blocker for #43918?
Oh, sorry, I'm an idiot #43918 is already merged. :-)
Nevertheless, I'll get the import linter and cleanup done shortly.
I should also mention import-graph#168 and import-graph#170 for #min_imports, though really I should add more tests. :)

Actually @Kim Morrison re: normalizing imports as a linter, would you mind if I just refactor mathlib's header linter to use import graph right now? How far have you gotten in the past half hour? (I know you work quickly... :) )

Reason being, I was responsible for the previous header linter refactor and we've essentially upstreamed part of that to import graph now (and #norm_imports behind the scenes uses those upstreamed primitives too), so I'd like to tie it up in a bow. :)
And if I don't PR something tonight I'll relinquish it. XD
No problem if you're already going ahead and would like to PR, though.

I've made a PR at #44507, but unfortunately it needs the quick fix in import-graph#171 to correctly alphabetize imports. (I'm building locally using the branch of 171 to apply the normalizations, but this will go overnight.)

Fable is unhappy with import-graph#168 and import-graph#170. I've done a brief sanity check and pushed back on a few things, but I'm not sure how happy you are reading AI reviews, so for now I'll just leave its comments at this gist: https://gist.github.com/kim-em/386181838d9ef63a1d833241a92c5bb8

I can: 1. convert those to inline review comments, 2. let you handle them from the gist, or 3. digest them properly myself and comment humanly (eventually!), as you prefer.
I merged import-graph#171 and updated #44507 to use the default branch again.

I can handle them from the gist, thanks! :) Interesting, from skimming through, some of these are already documented + explained, some of these are very trivial (I forgot to import the test files, whoops!), and some of them are very good observations. :D Thanks! I'll handle them soon :)

#44512 applies the style guide rule to imports, so public imports come before imports, separated by a blank line (but we don't otherwise reorder, and we ignore all and meta modifiers, as currently the style guide is silent on that: let's keep that out of scope).
It would be great to be able to merge this asap, as obviously it will rot.

Okay, here the state of play:

  • import-graph#172 (minor API)
  • my #44503 (needs to wait for import-graph#172) adds a text-based CI linter (which can also apply the edits), that currently only runs on modified files, which ensures that public import comes before import, with a blank line
  • #44512 contains all the changes needed to bring Mathlib into conformance
  • Thomas' #44507 adds a syntax linter that does pretty much the same thing, but also alphabetizes and cares about all and meta for sorting purposes. It runs everywhere, so will fail right now.
I think we probably should just close #44503, and go with Thomas' version.

But there's a decision to make here: Thomas' linter currently alphabetizes (and takes into account all and meta). However this isn't justified by the current style guide, which I read as being prescriptive about the public import vs import split, but only says to try to alphabetize.

I realise this is all tedious bikeshedding, but I would really like to get this decided, and no longer have to have conversations about this, and instead have linters enforce anything we want enforced, and no one to complain about anything that is not enforced by linters.
In particular, I think we should either lint for alphabetization, or remove the "try" clause.

By the way, my local build completed, so #44513 applies all of the "fancy" suggestions. :) I agree we ought to decide on what we really want before merging it, and ensure our linters are synchronized with our style conventions both ways, whatever we decide! :)
I've made a PR to blame-ignore the changes from #44512:
#44515

Kim Morrison said:

I think we should either lint for alphabetization, or remove the "try" clause.

AFAIK the issue is that alphabetizing breaks mathlib, and can affect performance. If possible, I think linting + some -- sort: ignore comment like Shake uses is the best solution. Could AIs figure out exactly where we need ignore comments?

Oh it seems everything is fine (see bench in #44513), I wonder what changed since #42111.
Previous discussion: #mathlib4 > Technical Debt Counters @ 💬
..alphabetisising breaks Mathlib?

I can't see discussion of alphabetisisation I'm the linked comment (might just be the mobile app acting up)
I think we should enforce it if possible because it gives us a unique layout for a given set of imports
(am less concerned with what exactly that layout is)

I think it's because the order matters for registering instances and simp lemmas
#mathlib4 > Alphabetical listing of imports @ 💬
Maybe fixing diamonds fixed this, or maybe it never broke and I'm misremembering
I wish we could have less churn in the import list when the review queue / maintainer queue is long :sweat_smile:Resolving conflicts is not particularly fun

Personally, I like the scenario of all imports being alphabetised: it's a simple rule, can be enforced mechanically and frees us from ever to discuss this again. This requires fixing any issues such large-scale alphabetisation reveals (such as, instance search time-outs or slow-downs), but I review such fixes as positive anyway. Assuming this can be done (which I am somewhat optimistic about), I think we should do this.
For the record: this is also discussed in the private mathlib reviewers stream. So far, all arguments made there are also reflected here, and the voice so far are in favour of this change.
One question that should be clarified is if shake will enforce such ordering. Of course, shake's behaviour and the style guide should be compatible.

Even if shake ignores it we could shake; sort in CI, right?
(although running skimmer in CI might be unprecedented)
I guess. But it would be nicer if shake didn't suggest imports going against mathlib's style guide.
If we decide on the "fully ordered" scenario, another option for handling shake --fix is that Kim could update #44503 so that we can use the same formatting in CI tooling via the text-based linter :)

Weiyi Wang said:

I wish we could have less churn in the import list when the review queue / maintainer queue is long :sweat_smile:Resolving conflicts is not particularly fun

Alphabetisising will reduce churn because it will guarantee that a given set of imports is written uniquely going forward
